subject: Chemistry
title: PFAS: Forever Chemicals in Your Blood
description: A quick win: understand PFAS: Forever Chemicals in Your Blood.

hook.text: PFAS chemicals are in 98% of Americans' blood. They're called 'forever chemicals' because they virtually never break down.

buildup.text: PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) have carbon-fluorine bonds—the strongest bond in organic chemistry.

discovery.text: They repel water and oil, making them ideal for non-stick pans, waterproof clothing, and firefighting foam.

twist.text: PFAS accumulate in the body and are linked to cancer, thyroid disease, and immune suppression. DuPont hid the data for decades.

climax.text: The EPA set near-zero limits for PFAS in drinking water in 2024. Cleanup will cost an estimated $400 billion.

punchline.text: Chemistry's strongest bond made the hardest pollution to clean. Forever means forever.

quiz.question: Why are PFAS called 'forever chemicals'?
options: Their carbon-fluorine bonds are nearly unbreakable in the environment
They glow permanently under UV light
They are radioactive with extremely long half-lives

details.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are synthetic chemicals whose carbon-fluorine bonds are so strong that they persist in the environment and human bodies indefinitely..
details.whyItMatters: PFAS exposure is linked to cancer, thyroid disease, and immune suppression. Their virtually indestructible chemistry means contamination is essentially permanent without active remediation.
takeaways: PFAS are called forever chemicals because they do not break down naturally
They are found in the blood of over 98% of Americans tested
Carbon-fluorine bonds are the strongest in organic chemistry

faq.question: Why are PFAS so difficult to destroy?
faq.answer: The carbon-fluorine bond is the strongest single bond in organic chemistry, requiring extreme conditions to break. PFAS resist heat, acids, bases, and microbial degradation..

faq.question: What everyday products contain PFAS chemicals?
faq.answer: PFAS are found in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, stain-resistant carpet treatments, food packaging, dental floss, some cosmetics, and aqueous firefighting foam. Their water- and grease-repelling properties made them commercially attractive across thousands of consumer products.
